finding.claim: The /mirror endpoint fetches a user-supplied URL after only a weak hostname check. The check uses host.endswith("example.com") with no leading dot, and the defined ALLOWED_SUFFIX (".example.com") is never used. An attacker can register or use a host like evilexample.com or attackerexample.com, which passes the check, and make the server issue requests to it. Redirects are not constrained either, but httpx does not follow them by default, so that is not the main issue. The scheme is also unrestricted (any http/https URL passes). Resolved IPs are not checked, so an allowed-looking domain that resolves to an internal address (DNS rebinding or attacker-controlled DNS) reaches internal services. Only the response length is returned, so this is a blind or limited-read SSRF.
finding.source: Query parameter `url` of GET /mirror (mirror.py:11), controlled by any unauthenticated client

trace.note: url taken directly from the query string
check is host.endswith("example.com"), which also accepts evilexample.com; ALLOWED_SUFFIX at line 7 is unused
the original, unmodified url is passed to c.get(url)

finding.guards_checked: Only the endswith("example.com") hostname check at line 13. It has no dot boundary, no scheme restriction, no port restriction, no DNS or IP resolution check, and no authentication. The /ping endpoint (line 23) uses a hardcoded URL and is not vulnerable.

verdict.guard_found: Only host.endswith("example.com") at mirror.py:13 (suffix check without dot boundary); ALLOWED_SUFFIX at line 7 is unused; no auth, scheme, or IP checks.
